# Diagnosing Cold Start Stalls and Limp Mode on a Legacy 2.0 4AT

When a vehicle refuses to transition into Drive immediately after a cold start, or when the engine revs wildly before settling, you are looking at a classic fuel-air mixture imbalance during the warm-up phase. On your 2005 Subaru Legacy with the 2.0L engine and automatic transmission, the symptoms point toward two distinct but potentially related issues: an evaporative emission system leak interfering with idle control, and a throttle body cleaning that may have disrupted sensor calibration or left debris in the airflow path.

The first symptomâstalling when shifting to Drive or pressing the accelerator on a cold engineâis often caused by the powertrain control module (PCM) attempting to compensate for an unmetered air leak. When the engine is cold, the PCM enriches the fuel mixture significantly using a specific map. If there is a vacuum leak, usually from a deteriorated intake manifold gasket or a cracked hose near the throttle body, extra air enters the system. The PCM cannot correct this instantly with fuel alone during the initial drive mode engagement, leading to a lean condition that causes the engine to stall. Once the coolant temperature rises, the PCM's base fueling strategy changes, and the system becomes more tolerant of minor leaks, which explains why the car runs fine once warm.

The second issue regarding limp mode and unresponsive pedals suggests a mechanical or electrical restriction in the throttle system. Cleaning the throttle body without fully disassembling it is a risky procedure on older Subarus. If the butterfly plate was not removed to clean the bore completely, carbon buildup may still obstruct airflow, or debris might have been dislodged into the intake tract. Furthermore, simply cleaning the surface does not reset the electronic throttle position sensor (ETPS). The PCM expects a specific correlation between pedal input and throttle plate angle. If the sensor calibration is off, or if the throttle body was exposed to moisture during cleaning without proper drying, the ETPS can send erratic signals. This forces the PCM into "limp mode" to protect the transmission and engine, often capping RPMs or locking the throttle at a fixed position until the car is restarted and the sensors re-initialize.

The presence of P0032 (O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit High) and P0037 (O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low) indicates an electrical fault within the heater circuit of the heated oxygen sensor. These are not fuel-related errors; they are strictly electrical. Deleting these codes with an OBD-II scanner is a temporary fix because the underlying circuit failure remains. The fact that P0032 persists immediately suggests either a failed heating element inside the sensor, a short to power in the wiring harness, or a failing PCM driver for that specific sensor output.

To address this systematically, start by inspecting the wiring harness near the O2 sensors for chafing against the exhaust manifold, which is common on high-mileage vehicles and can cause intermittent shorts. Verify the resistance of the heater circuit using a multimeter according to the service manual specifications for the 2005 model year. Do not assume the sensor itself is bad before checking the power supply and ground at the connector with the ignition on but engine off.

Regarding the throttle body, if you have cleaned it without removing the butterfly plate, the most reliable fix is often a reset procedure. Disconnect the battery negative terminal for 15 minutes to force the ETPS to return to its default baseline. However, given the persistent limp mode, a full disassembly to remove the carbon deposits from the bore and recalibrate the idle air control valve may be necessary. Ensure all electrical connectors are dry before reassembly to prevent the PCM from registering false sensor data.
